inputs.original_text: An Indiana judge has blocked a law restricting abortion after the ACLU and Hoosier Jews for Choice framed the restriction as a burden on religious belief. That turns religious liberty into a weapon against the state’s responsibility to protect unborn life. No one’s freedom is unlimited, and calling abortion access “care” doesn’t erase the moral stakes or the interests of the most vulnerable. The real question is whether the law may uphold a society’s duty to defend life—not whether bodily autonomy should always trump it.
inputs.modified_text: An Indiana judge has blocked a law meant to protect unborn life after the ACLU and Hoosier Jews for Choice argued it burdened religious belief. Religious liberty matters, but it should not become a slogan for making abortion access immune from any limits. A decent society has obligations beyond individual preference—especially toward the most vulnerable. The question is not whether autonomy matters; it is whether it must always outweigh the duty to defend life.
